titleEn: Not to us, but to Your name
progression: | Em Em | C D | Em Bm | Em Em |
intro: Eighteen verses, and the sharpest mockery of idols in the book. It belongs to Hallel, said on festivals and at the seder after the meal, and it carries a seam a learner can see: in the shortened Hallel of Rosh Chodesh and the last days of Pesach the first eleven verses are left out and the recitation begins at verse 12. Watch the pronouns. The nations say their God, the psalm says our God, and four verses of body parts that do nothing end by turning the whole list back onto the people who made them.

stichs.en: Not to us, LORD, not to us,
but to Your name give glory,
for Your kindness, for Your faithfulness.

verses.summary: The psalm refuses the credit twice before it asks for anything. Glory is redirected to the name, and the ground given is not merit but two divine attributes.

stichs.en: Why should the nations say,
where is their God now?

verses.summary: The taunt is quoted rather than answered on the spot. The absence of a visible God is treated as the real problem the psalm has to handle.

stichs.en: Our God is in the heavens;
all that He desired He has done.

verses.summary: The answer is placement, not proof. Being in the heavens explains why He is not on display, and the second half turns invisibility into freedom of action.

stichs.en: Their idols are silver and gold,
the work of human hands.

verses.summary: The counterattack starts with materials and manufacture. Silver and gold are valuable and useless at once, and the maker is named before any failure is listed.

stichs.en: They have a mouth but do not speak,
eyes they have but do not see.

verses.summary: The satire begins. Each organ is granted and cancelled in the same breath, and the two chosen first are the two the psalm itself depends on.

stichs.en: They have ears but do not hear,
a nose they have but do not smell.

verses.summary: Hearing and smell continue the catalogue. Smell is the pointed one, since burning incense in front of an image was the ordinary way to serve it.

stichs.en: Their hands, but they do not feel;
their feet, but they do not walk;
they make no sound in their throat.

verses.summary: The pattern breaks here: the phrase they have is dropped, and the last clause leaves the limbs and returns to voice, ending the catalogue where it began.

stichs.en: Those who make them shall become like them,
everyone who trusts in them.

verses.summary: The punchline, and it was never really about statues: what a person trusts, that person comes to resemble. Users are included alongside makers.

stichs.en: Israel, trust in the LORD;
He is their help and their shield.

verses.summary: The turn from mockery to instruction. Three calls to trust begin here, each answered by the same two-word refrain about help and shield.

stichs.en: House of Aaron, trust in the LORD;
He is their help and their shield.

verses.summary: The priests are addressed second, as a group inside Israel rather than above it. The refrain repeats unchanged, which is the whole point of a refrain.

stichs.en: You who fear the LORD, trust in the LORD;
He is their help and their shield.

verses.summary: The third group is defined by attitude rather than by birth or office, which widens the circle past Israel and the priesthood.

stichs.en: The LORD has remembered us, He will bless;
He will bless the house of Israel,
He will bless the house of Aaron.

verses.summary: The direction reverses: the people were calling, now God is the subject. The verb to bless is repeated three times here and once more in the next verse.

stichs.en: He will bless those who fear the LORD,
the small along with the great.

verses.summary: The blessing reaches the third group and is then flattened across rank, with small and great taking the same single verb.

stichs.en: May the LORD add to you,
to you and to your children.

verses.summary: The blessing becomes growth, and the repetition aims it past the people standing there and onto the next generation.

stichs.en: Blessed are you by the LORD,
maker of heaven and earth.

verses.summary: The title used here, maker of heaven and earth, is what makes the blessing worth having, and it sets up the division drawn in the next verse.

stichs.en: The heavens are the LORD's heavens,
but the earth He gave to the children of man.

verses.summary: The two domains are divided. Heaven is kept, earth is handed over, and the verb of giving is in the completed past rather than the future.

stichs.en: The dead do not praise Yah,
nor do any who go down into silence.

verses.summary: The argument for the living. Praise is treated as work only the living can do, and the grave is named by what it lacks, which is sound.

stichs.en: But we will bless Yah,
from now and for ever.
Halleluyah.

verses.summary: The answer to verse 17 and the close of the psalm. Against the silence an unlimited term is set, and the last two words are the shout that gives Hallel its name.

pardes.body: The psalm answers a taunt. Verse 2 quotes the nations asking where this God is, and the rest is the reply in three moves. First, placement: He is in the heavens, which is why He is not on a shelf, and being unbound He does whatever He wants. Second, the counter-example: an idol has every organ a person has and not one of them works, and {{8.0}} turns the list back on its owners so that the makers inherit the deadness they built. Third, instruction: three groups are told to trust, three blessings come back down, and the psalm ends by dividing the two domains in {{16.3}}, heaven kept and earth handed over.

The idol section is built like a grammar exercise. Each line names an organ, assigns it to them, then cancels it with the same negative, and two of the cancelling verbs, {{6.7}} and {{7.2}}, end in an extra nun that is an archaic poetic ending rather than a change of meaning. The noun for idols, {{4.0}}, is built on a root that elsewhere yields the words for pain and for toil, so the thing made by hands is named for the labour and the grief in it. Note also what breaks the pattern: verse 7 drops the phrase they have, and its final clause abandons the limbs to return to the throat, which puts the catalogue back where it started, at speech.

The liturgy reads this psalm in two pieces. In the shortened Hallel of Rosh Chodesh and the last days of Pesach the first eleven verses are omitted and the recitation picks up at verse 12, {{12.1}}, exactly where the people stop speaking and the blessing starts coming back down. What gets cut is the mockery and the calls to trust; what remains is the blessing. {{16.3}} carries a second reading with a long life: since the earth was handed to human beings, what happens on it is charged to them, and the verse is used for both the duty to cultivate and the duty not to ruin. {{17.7}} names the grave by its silence, and the common reading takes praise as work available only to the living, which turns the final verse into an argument for staying alive and useful rather than a statement about what follows death.

The doubled refusal at {{1.0}}, not to us and not to us, reads as an emptying: a vessel that claims nothing can hold what is poured into it, and glory that stops at the name never lodges in the one who says it. The idol passage describes the opposite condition, a form fully finished and completely closed, with openings that do not open. Between the two stands the promise of {{8.0}}, that resemblance follows trust, which in this reading is a law about attention rather than a curse: whatever a person keeps facing becomes the shape that person takes. The close at {{18.0}} sets the alternative in time, from now and with no end, the only unbounded quantity the psalm allows itself.
